## Add the workflow

Save this as `.github/workflows/laya-triage.yml`. It triages new issues, supports a manual backfill, and warms the caches twice a week:

```yaml
{{consumer_workflow}}
```

`{{tag}}` is a tag, and tags can move: for anything beyond a trial, replace it with the full commit SHA of the release and keep the tag as a comment (`uses: Prasanna-KS-85/laya-triage@<full commit SHA> # {{tag}}`; see §7.6 of [`PROJECT_SPEC.md`](../PROJECT_SPEC.md)). This prints the commit SHA of the release:

```bash
{{ls_remote}}
```

The Action runs on Linux X64 only. It was tested on `ubuntu-24.04`; `ubuntu-latest` moves to a newer image on {{ubuntu_switch_date}}, so pin `ubuntu-24.04` if you want the tested one.

If you only want new issues triaged, without the backfill and the cache warm-up, the [README](../README.md#path-a-the-github-action) shows a minimal version of this workflow.

## Permissions

The job needs `issues: write` and `contents: read`, nothing else. `issues: write` lets the Action add labels and, if enabled, comment; `contents: read` lets the checkout step read your `.github/laya-triage.yml`. The built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` is enough: no personal token and no Hugging Face token (the model is public). Without `issues: write` the run fails with a message naming the missing permission.

## Create the labels

The Action skips a label that does not exist, unless you set `behaviour.create_missing_labels`:

```bash
{{label_cmds}}
```

## Warm the caches once

In the Actions tab, run the workflow manually with `warm-cache` ticked. It validates the config, loads the model and saves the model and dependency caches, but reads no issues and makes no GitHub API call. Issues-triggered runs can restore these caches but cannot save them, which is why the schedule in the example exists.

On the sandbox runner a first run with cold caches took {{cold}} and a run with restored caches {{warm}} ([runtime details](DEEP_DIVE.md#runtime-and-the-latency-probe)).

## First run: stay in dry-run and read the job summaries

The default mode is `{{mode}}`. Open a few issues, or run the workflow manually with a `backfill-count` to classify the most recent open issues, then read the decision table in each run's job summary: label, probabilities, and whether the Action would apply or escalate. Compare it with what you would have done.

Advice for the first week:

- Leave the defaults alone and collect a few dozen dry-run decisions before you change anything.
- Check the `bug` decisions the Action would apply: that is the only label it applies by itself with the default thresholds, and its precision on your repository can differ from the benchmark.
- Expect most issues to be escalated. That is the gate working, not a failure.
- Each run also uploads a JSONL log as an artifact (decisions and probabilities, no issue text) if you want to tally them.

## Backfill

Run the workflow manually (`workflow_dispatch`) with `backfill-count` set to a number of issues: the Action classifies that many of the most recent open issues. Backfill runs are dry-run unless you set the `mode` input to `apply` for that run. Issues that already carry one of the three type labels or the escalation label are skipped, so a second backfill does not repeat work.

## Switch to apply

Only when you are happy with what dry-run showed, add `.github/laya-triage.yml`:

```yaml
behaviour:
  mode: apply
```

With the shipped thresholds ({{thresholds_text}}), only `bug` is ever applied automatically. `feature` and `question` are always escalated, because no threshold on validation data reached the precision target for them (a threshold of {{never}} means never).

## Escalation comments

By default an escalated issue only gets the `{{escalate_label}}` label. Set `behaviour.comment_on_escalate: true` to also post one fixed-text comment with the top two guesses. The text is fixed in the code; only label names and percentages are filled in, so it never repeats the issue. For the sandbox fixtures in the [README's worked example](../README.md#one-worked-example) it would read:

S02, `bug` below its threshold:

```text
{{s02_comment}}
```

S05, `question`, which is never auto-applied:

```text
{{s05_comment}}
```

## Troubleshooting

- **The run fails at once with "supports Linux X64 runners only".** The Action runs on Linux X64 only; use `ubuntu-24.04` or `ubuntu-latest`.
- **The run fails with a list of config keys.** `.github/laya-triage.yml` has an unknown key, a missing value or a wrong type. Fix the keys named in the message; nothing is guessed.
- **The run fails naming `issues: write`.** Add the `permissions` block from the workflow above.
- **The run succeeds but the summary says no issues were triaged.** A runtime problem (dependency install, model download, a timeout) was logged as a warning and the run ended successfully on purpose, so it never blocks your pipeline. Read the warning in the log; the next run usually succeeds. Set `behaviour.escalate_on_error: true` if such issues should get the escalation label.
- **A label was not added and the log warns about a missing label.** Create the labels (above) or set `behaviour.create_missing_labels: true`.
- **Every run is slow.** The caches are cold or were evicted after a week unused. Run the workflow once with `warm-cache` ticked and keep the schedule trigger.
- **An issue was skipped.** Pull requests, issues opened by the authors in `behaviour.skip_authors`, and issues that already carry a type label or the escalation label are skipped by design; the job summary gives the reason.
- **Nothing changed on the issue.** The default mode is dry-run. See [Switch to apply](#switch-to-apply).
